channel.title: Meal_planning on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Meal_planning on Best of AI

item.title: Nutrium
item.description:
Nutrium helps nutrition professionals run a practice. They manage clients, schedule appointments, and keep records of measurements and goals, while clients use an app to log meals and see their plan. A food database with nutrient data supports analysis and meal planning.

AI speeds up plan creation by proposing menus that fit a client’s calorie and nutrient targets and preferences, which the dietitian then adjusts. Reports and communication tools keep clients engaged between visits.

item.title: Vivino
item.description:
Vivino started as a wine label scanner. A user photographs a bottle, and the app recognizes it, showing the average rating, tasting notes, price ranges, and what other drinkers say. This helps shoppers choose in stores and restaurants.

The app has become a marketplace as well, where users can buy wines from partner merchants. A taste profile learns from your ratings and recommends bottles, and features include food pairing suggestions and a cellar to track wines.

item.title: Lifesum
item.description:
Lifesum helps people understand what they eat. Users set a goal such as weight loss, maintenance, or muscle gain, then log food and drink by searching, scanning barcodes, or snapping photos. The app shows calories, macros, and nutrient balance, and gives feedback through scores and summaries.

Meal plans and recipes support particular diets, such as low carb, Mediterranean, or intermittent fasting. Integrations with fitness trackers and health apps bring in activity data. AI features help with logging foods from photos and offer personalized suggestions.

item.title: FoodDocs
item.description:
FoodDocs is a digital food safety system. A restaurant, producer, or caterer answers questions about what it makes and how, and the software generates a food safety plan with hazard analysis and control points, along with the daily tasks to carry it out. Staff complete checklists on a phone or tablet.

Monitoring features include temperature logging, cleaning schedules, and alerts when tasks are missed or readings are out of range. Records are stored and ready for inspectors, and AI helps adapt the plan when menus or processes change. Sensors can send temperature readings automatically.

item.title: PlantNet
item.description: Pl@ntNet lets anyone identify a plant by taking a photo. You photograph a leaf, flower, fruit, or bark, and the app compares it with a large reference collection and returns a list of likely species with confidence scores and similar images. It covers wild plants and many cultivated ones, with regional floras for different parts of the world, and works best when you provide several views of the same plant.

item.title: SideChef
item.description:
SideChef is built for people who want help in the kitchen. Each recipe is broken into short steps with photos or video, so you can follow along while cooking, and hands-free voice control and timers keep you moving without touching your phone with messy hands. Recipes cover a wide range of cuisines and diets, and you can scale servings, swap ingredients, and save favorites.

Planning features reduce the work around cooking. Meal plans suggest weekly menus based on tastes and dietary needs, and shopping lists are built automatically from chosen recipes, with options to order groceries through delivery partners. The app also works with smart kitchen devices, and AI helps personalize recommendations and adjust plans over time.

item.title: Whisk
item.description:
Whisk started as an independent app for collecting recipes. You could save dishes from any food site into one library, group them into collections, plan meals for the week, and turn the ingredients into a shopping list that could be sent to grocery delivery services. A browser extension made saving a recipe a single click.

Samsung bought the company and renamed the app Samsung Food, and the whisk.com address now leads to the new brand. The app keeps the same core features and adds AI help, such as adjusting a recipe to dietary needs, suggesting meals from what you have, and generating plans. It also connects with Samsung’s smart appliances, though it works without them on phones and the web.

item.title: Yuka
item.description:
Yuka makes reading labels simpler. You scan the barcode of a food or personal care product with your phone, and the app returns a score with color coding and an explanation of what affects it. For food, the score considers nutritional quality, additives, and whether the product is organic. For cosmetics, it flags ingredients seen as risky.

The app is built to help shoppers choose. When a product scores poorly, Yuka suggests better alternatives in the same category, and you can keep a history of what you scanned. It does not accept advertising or payments from brands for ratings, and it funds itself through its premium subscription, which adds features like searching without a barcode and offline use.
